messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 23
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: UX Designer
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 75

# The Weight of a Moment

Priya is twenty-three years old, newly married, and spends her days designing digital experiences meant to feel intuitive and safe. There is a quiet irony in this that she does not miss. She thinks about it sometimes when she is sitting at her desk, moving elements around a screen, asking herself whether a user will feel confused or at ease. She knows, more than most people her age, how quickly safety can collapse into something irreversible.

Fourteen months ago, Priya was driving home from a late evening at the studio where she worked at the time. She was not speeding. She had not been drinking. She was tired, the way young professionals in demanding jobs are chronically tired, and she glanced down at her phone for what she estimates was two seconds — maybe three. When she looked up, a cyclist was directly in front of her. She braked hard but not hard enough. The impact was not loud the way she had always imagined accidents would be. It was brief and dull, and then there was a man lying in the road.

He survived. He lost partial function in his left hand and sustained a serious spinal injury that required months of rehabilitation. Priya learned these details through legal proceedings she was required to attend. She sat in those rooms feeling like something that should not be allowed to occupy space.

The criminal matter was eventually resolved without charges, a determination that brought her family enormous relief and brought Priya almost nothing. She returned to work within two weeks because staying home felt worse. She changed jobs shortly afterward, telling herself it was a natural career move, though she understood on some level that she needed a new desk, new colleagues, a new city if possible. She and her husband Rohan had been married only four months when the accident happened. He is patient and loving and she finds it increasingly difficult to let him be either of those things to her.

At night, Priya does not sleep so much as she waits. She lies still and the accident replays with a fidelity that feels almost technical — the exact quality of the evening light, the sound, the shape of the man's body against the pavement. Sometimes the sequence changes and she sees his face before the impact, looking at her, which is not what actually happened. She wakes from these images at two or three in the morning and moves to the living room so that Rohan will not notice.

During the day, she avoids driving entirely. She takes rideshares, the subway, long walks that make her late to meetings. When she is a passenger in someone else's car she grips the door handle and monitors the road with an attention that exhausts her. Her colleagues have noticed that she seems distracted. She has missed deadlines she would never have missed before. Sitting in front of wireframes and user-flow diagrams, she sometimes finds that twenty minutes have passed and she cannot account for them.

She has told almost no one the full story. Her parents know there was an accident. Rohan knows the facts but not the texture of what she carries. She has become careful and slightly formal with him, as though proximity to someone who loves her might expose how thoroughly she believes she does not deserve it. When he asks how she is doing, she says she is tired. This is true. It is also the smallest possible version of the truth.

What Priya returns to, again and again, is not the legal question of fault, which was examined and settled. It is a different question, one that has no proceeding and no resolution. She had looked down. She had made a choice, ordinary and thoughtless, the kind every person makes a dozen times a day. And in the space of two or three seconds, a man's life changed permanently. She lives now in the aftermath of that interval, measuring everything against it, unable to locate a version of herself that existed before she knew what she was capable of.
